events.text: A dock hand hands you a folded card in handwriting like a ransom note. DINNER. TONIGHT. DON'T BRING ANYTHING. IF YOU BRING SOMETHING I'LL KNOW IT'S AN APOLOGY. - M. Ma Gantry lives in the oldest hull in the Rusthold, a rust-red freighter called the Mother Plate, the first wreck anyone ever welded another wreck to. The door is a hatch with a cat flap. Inside is a kitchen, a long table, a kettle that has seen things, and a very small woman stirring a very big pot with something that used to be an oar. Her sleeves are rolled up. She does not have the clipboard. It is the first time you have seen her without it, and you do not know where to look.

outcomes.text: The stew is good. It is so good that you forget to be wary. Ma watches you eat with her chin in her hand and, when you have finished, takes your bowl and says, to the pot, 'Well, that's one that eats.' She writes a number on the table in chalk, rubs it out, and knocks a hundred and fifty off yours without looking up. 'Don't tell anyone,' she says. 'It'd ruin me.'

choices.text: Ask why she lends hulls instead of selling them.

outcomes.text: Ma stirs for a long time. 'Because a hull you owe me for,' she says, 'is a name on my wall. And a name on my wall gets looked for. You think I'm in it for the money? I know every name that owes me, and when one stops answering, I send a boat. Forty-one boats, so far.' The oar goes round. 'Nobody sends a boat for somebody who paid cash.' She looks at you. 'That's the debt. That's all the debt ever was.'

choices.text: [Fenn] Offer to audit her books, as a courtesy.

outcomes.text: Ma laughs like a bolt coming loose and slides the ledger across, which nobody has done in forty years. Your Fenn reads three pages and goes very quiet. The numbers are wrong, on purpose, in the same direction, every month. 'It's a roll call,' says your Fenn. 'Every line is a person who's still flying.' 'Put that back,' says Ma, gently. 'You'll upset the cousins.' She takes two hundred off, for the discretion, and gives your Fenn the good spoon.

choices.text: Pay her a hundred, in person, on the spot. (100 credits)

outcomes.text: Ma takes the hundred in both hands, as if it were still warm. 'In person,' she says. 'Nobody does it in person.' She counts it twice, out loud, then rounds it up in her own favour and her own head, and takes two hundred off the number to even things out. Her eyes are wet. She is blaming the onions.

choices.text: Thank her for the invitation, and leave. Dinners are for people with less debt.

outcomes.text: 'Smart,' says Ma, without turning round. 'Stupid. Smart.' The cat flap swings behind you. The smell of the stew follows you all the way to the dock, which is its own kind of invoice.

events.text: The Concord's flagship has not moved in forty years, and she is the size of the Rusthold. CS-001 Patience: every light on, every flag flying, every gun under its cover, and on her long white bridge a captain's chair turned to face the empty windows, waiting for orders from the Lattice Authority. No orders have come. She has not stopped listening. Along her flank, in letters four metres high, someone has painted a single word: STANDING BY.

choices.text: Hail her with the old Concord courtesy code. (Concord trust)

outcomes.text: A hatch opens in her flank with a long, relieved sigh. The ship's mind, a recording of Captain Adaeze Okoro, welcomes you aboard in the voice of a woman who has rehearsed a welcome for forty years and means to get it right. 'Visitors,' she says. 'I am so sorry about the dust.' She gives you the freedom of the ship, a tour of the bridge, a box of circuit boards the Fleet never got to use, and a drawing taped to the captain's chair of a smaller ship with a name on its hull: CS-002 Forbearance. 'My little sister,' says Okoro. 'In the yard at Meridian. Never launched. Would you mind?'

choices.text: Breach a service hatch and slip aboard.

outcomes.text: An alarm sounds. 'ALERT. UNREGISTERED VISITOR. Please fill in a visitor form.' The form is on a clipboard by the door. You fill it in. The ship lets you in with the air of a customs officer who would be delighted to be wrong. You leave with the circuit boards, the drawing and a small, fussy reputation.

A boarding gantry, forty years old and hungry, takes a swing at you in the dark. Everyone lives. Nobody is happy. The ship, mortified, apologises on every speaker until you are out of range, and then, you suspect, for some time after.

choices.text: [Mechanical] Speak machine to the ship's mind.

outcomes.text: Your Gauntling puts a hand on the bridge panel and says something that isn't words. The ship's mind answers in kind. 'No one has spoken to me in a voice I could parse since the Snap,' it says, and the whole ship quietly turns its lights down to the colour of a lamp on a table. It opens everything. It gives you the best of what it has: three boards, a drawing of a smaller ship, and a long, quiet, grateful goodbye.

choices.text: Salute and leave her to wait.

outcomes.text: You salute. Somewhere in her long white bridge, you swear, a captain's chair turns an inch to watch you go. STANDING BY, says the hull, and goes on saying it, long after you are out of sight.

events.text: You fly in through the break where a ship used to be. Inside the shell a Dead Gate is a cathedral nobody finished: ribs of dead lattice, white as bone, rising out of sight in every direction, and between them a silence with a texture, like a sheet pulled tight. Your suit lights find the first rib and lose the last. Somewhere ahead a drop of old condensation falls, and the sound arrives a full second late. The gate is not quite dead. It is dead the way a bell is quiet.

choices.text: Walk the ribs by suit light.

outcomes.text: You walk for an hour. The ribs bend away from you as you pass, as if shy. In the walls, every metre or so, there is alloy: warm, heavy, the colour of old brass. You take what you can carry, and you stand for a moment at the centre of the thing, where the sky should be. Something very large is not looking at you. It is the nicest thing anyone has ever not done.

A rib lets go of its old tension with a sound like a ship's bell, and a plate comes down across your path. Everyone is fine; nobody is quite as fine as they were. The alloy is in your hand, and a long note is still ringing in your teeth.

choices.text: [Basalt] Take off your suit. You don't need it.

outcomes.text: Your Basalt steps out of the airlock in nothing but his skin and walks the ribs like a man in his own front hall. 'I know this room,' he says. He does not say how. He lays a palm on a rib, and every light in the shell comes on, softly, for the length of a breath, and goes out again. 'They are all still here,' he says, 'in the walls.' He picks the alloy out of the ribs with perfect tact, as if asking permission of each one.
You back out the way you came. Behind you the ribs settle, one by one, like an audience that has decided not to clap.

events.text: Deep in the Prism there is a room the acolytes call the Quiet Lab, which is the loudest room you have ever been in. It contains one thing: a model of a gate, no bigger than a hat, grown from crystal, with a small red light on its rim. 'Experiment 4411,' says the researcher who shows you in. Her name is Mira, and she has not slept since the experiment was new. 'We send a pulse. The gate answers. It has answered every pulse we have ever sent. Yesterday it answered one we had not sent yet.' She taps the rim. 'It is a timing fault,' she says, in the voice of a woman who has said it for years. 'Watch. I will send the pulse in nine seconds.'

outcomes.text: The light blinks before the pulse. Then again, and again. Mira lets you hold the model while it does it. It is warm, like a pet. The Lumen note, solemnly, that you are the first outsider to be allowed to hold it, and give you a shard of the cradle, the design of the thing that listens to it, and a look of such enormous relief that you understand how long they have been the only ones who knew.

choices.text: [Prismatic] Hold the model against your chest.

outcomes.text: Your Prismatic cradles the model against their chest. The light on its rim stops blinking. For a very long minute the model and the Prismatic hum together, in the same key, in unison. 'It answered,' whispers Mira, 'before I asked.' Her voice cracks. She has not been answered in her own key before, in all those years.

'Everything,' says Mira. 'It answers before we ask. As though it knew who would be asking. As though...' She stops. 'We think the Snap was a question, not a command. We think somebody asked, and the gate said yes. We just don't know to what.'

choices.text: Decline. It makes your teeth itch.

outcomes.text: 'It does that,' says Mira, sympathetic. 'It makes mine itch too. It is how we know it is working.'
